strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: detecting misleading creator intent in multimodal news, moving beyond surface-level cross-modal misalignment
High-quality dataset construction with rigorous filtering, systematic intent-guided generation, and strong human validation (99.2% accuracy, κ=0.877 for text)
Comprehensive evaluation of 14 state-of-the-art VLMs across three related tasks with both implication-oriented and consistency-oriented reasoning approaches
Insightful multi-faceted analysis revealing how VLMs rely on spurious cues (cross-modal consistency, stylistic signals, authenticity hints) rather than genuine intent understanding
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, complete appendices supporting reproducibility, and responsible disclosure plans
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark paper leveraging existing tools (GPT-4o, FLUX) with straightforward prompting-based evaluation; no new detection methods or solutions proposed
Synthetic data representativeness concerns: entire 12,000-instance dataset generated by LLMs; human validation only covers 2% of data; potential data leakage or model-specific artifacts not analyzed

Fuzzy task definitions: 'misleading' is subjective; Creator Desire Inference achieves poor performance (0-75.2% F1) with some models at 0%, but paper doesn't adequately discuss whether the task is well-posed

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; models run once with temperature=0; limited baselines including no human performance; key analyses use small sample sizes (200 samples for image generation)

Limited practical impact: no solutions proposed for identified problems; evaluation assumes trustworthy reference articles available, unrealistic in real-world deployment; benchmark limited to English, Western-centric news from VisualNews
Reference article dependency: evaluation setup assumes ground-truth context always available, contradicting real-world MMD scenarios where trusted references are rarely accessible
Moderate inter-annotator agreement for images (κ=0.703) and human validation limited to 2% of dataset raises questions about label quality at scale
No fine-tuning experiments: only prompt-based evaluation; no investigation of how models could be adapted for this task

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an underexplored gap: explicit modeling of misleading creator intent rather than surface-level cross-modal misalignment in multimodal misinformation detection
Large-scale resource with 12,000 systematically generated instances across 10 diverse news topics and high human validation quality (99.2% accuracy, κ=0.877 for text)
Comprehensive evaluation across 14 representative VLMs (proprietary, open-source, varying scales) providing broad empirical coverage

Valuable in-depth analysis in Section 5 systematically probing VLM failure modes, including image-text consistency masking deception, stylistic bias, and susceptibility to prompt-level authenticity cues
Responsible ethical considerations with reasonable mitigation strategies for potential misuse
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on synthetic data generated entirely through GPT-4o and FLUX raises fundamental ecological validity concerns; no validation on naturally occurring misinformation from social media platforms, limiting real-world applicability and generalization
Limited technical novelty: paper is purely a benchmark and analysis contribution with no new methods, detection algorithms, or solutions proposed to address the identified VLM limitations

Incomplete experimental rigor: single run per experiment (temperature=0), no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, error bars, or variance estimation; no human performance baselines provided, making task difficulty unclear
Synthetic data creates circular evaluation risk: using GPT-4o to generate misleading content then evaluating other VLMs' ability to detect it may introduce systematic biases and artifacts

Task design issues: vague operationalization of 'subtle' vs. 'significant' misleading intents, inconsistent evaluation approaches (I vs. C) that are fundamentally different tasks, and no ablation on reference article necessity
Reproducibility limitations: explicit withholding of data generation prompts (Section 3.3) despite promises to release data significantly limits verification and reproducibility

Analysis lacks depth on solutions: identifies problems (stylistic bias, prompt susceptibility, consistency-masking) but proposes no training strategies, robustness approaches, or mitigations; Section 5.2 on image generation is underdeveloped (only 200 samples)
Narrow scope and generalization concerns: limited to 10 VisualNews topics, only image/caption modifications tested, no evaluation on other platforms/languages, and no domain adaptation analysis

Missing critical experimental baselines: no human performance baselines for task difficulty calibration, no simple baseline comparisons (BERTScore, CLIP similarity), no fine-tuning experiments on specialized MMD models

Limited human validation coverage: only 2% of dataset human-validated, image validation shows moderate agreement (κ=0.703), and annotation conducted by only 3 graduate students limiting perspective diversity

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Shifts focus from surface-level cross-modal misalignment to understanding underlying misleading creator intent, addressing a genuine gap in MMD research with clear real-world relevance

Carefully constructed benchmark: Rigorous filtering based on journalism standards, diverse coverage (10 topics, 8 intent types), strong human validation (99.2% text accuracy, κ=0.877), and trustworthy grounding via VisualNews

Comprehensive evaluation: Systematically evaluates 14 representative VLMs across architectures with three complementary intent-centric tasks and multiple evaluation paradigms (implication vs. consistency-oriented)

Insightful and well-designed analysis: Section 5 effectively exposes model vulnerabilities through clever experiments (partial modality inputs, stylistic reframing, prompt-level hints, image quality variation) that reveal over-reliance on spurious cues

Clear presentation and ethical considerations: Well-written with effective visualizations; thoughtfully addresses potential harms through anonymization, restricted data access, and withholding generation prompts
weaknesses: Synthetic data generation limitations: All misleading content created by GPT-4o following instructions, not by real human creators; real misinformation may employ different tactics. While human validation is strong (99.2%), this doesn't guarantee capturing real-world misinformation diversity or sophistication. No comparative analysis with actual misinformation campaigns

Creator intent framework not validated against real creators: The 2D framework (desired influence + execution plan) lacks validation that it actually corresponds to how real misinformation creators conceptualize their objectives. The 8 intent categories are somewhat coarse and may not be comprehensive

Insufficient statistical rigor: Critical limitation—experiments run only once with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing. Only 3 annotators for human evaluation. Image quality analysis (Section 5.2) uses only 200 samples. This is especially problematic for synthetic data where variation could affect conclusions

Task 3 (Creator Desire Inference) shows poor performance (0-75 F1%) and unclear utility: Multi-label prediction from predefined categories appears overly restrictive. More importantly, practical value is unclear—how would systems use creator desire predictions for actual content moderation?

Limited practical application discussion: Paper motivates intent understanding as important but doesn't deeply explore how systems would operationalize intent predictions or integrate into content moderation workflows. Unclear what downstream actions systems would take based on detected intent

Non-misleading cases show ceiling effects: Text instances achieve 78-100% accuracy across models, suggesting task imbalance or that reference articles provide excessive signal. Limits ability to distinguish model capabilities

Reproducibility concerns: Generation prompts intentionally withheld (understandable for safety but limits reproducibility). Dataset not yet available. Limited details on image generation specifics (FLUX variant, exact prompts)

strengths: Novel problem framing: Focuses on misleading creator intent rather than surface-level misalignment, addressing an important yet underexplored aspect of multimodal misinformation detection grounded in communication theory

Exceptionally thorough human validation: 99.2% accuracy for text, 89.2% for images with high inter-annotator agreement; additional validation of data realism (98%+), and intent alignment (92%+) goes beyond typical dataset work

Comprehensive benchmark design: 12,000 samples grounded in trustworthy reference articles across 10 domains, with both text and image manipulations at multiple severity levels supporting three complementary tasks

Extensive empirical evaluation: 14 diverse VLMs evaluated with two reasoning paradigms; insightful failure analysis reveals model reliance on surface-level cues (semantic consistency, stylistic polish, spurious authenticity hints) rather than genuine intent reasoning
Demonstrated generalization: Fine-tuning on DECEPTIONDECODED transfers improvements to external MMD benchmark (MMFakeBench), suggesting utility beyond specific benchmark tasks
Strong reproducibility: Detailed appendices with prompts, model cards, evaluation protocols; reasonable ethical stance on withholding generation prompts while releasing data
weaknesses: Synthetic data with potential circularity and generalization concerns: All content generated by GPT-4o, with ground truth intent derived from the same models used to generate content. Unclear if findings generalize to real misinformation campaigns or different synthesis methods. No analysis of distribution shift from authentic misinformation.

Narrow scope limiting applicability: Restricted to subtle caption/image manipulations within single-event contexts. Excludes identifiable individuals (common in real-world misinformation) and other important types (deepfakes, multi-event composites, sequential manipulation). Claims of generality are overstated.

Task design relies on simulated intent: Ground truth intent labels from GPT-4o simulation rather than actual creators. While human validation confirms consistency, indirect validation of 'simulated intent = true creator intent' is questionable. Creates potential circularity where VLMs struggle with GPT-generated intent.

Practical applicability concerns: Consistency-oriented approach (better performing) requires trustworthy reference articles, unavailable in real deployments. Performance drops substantially without context (Table 4). Benchmark assumes idealized information environment not reflective of real-world scenarios.

Missing human performance baseline: No human accuracy reported on these tasks. Without baseline, unclear whether modest model performance (84-86% intent detection, 75% desire inference F1) represents genuine difficulty or task design issues. Prevents assessment of room for improvement.

Creator desire inference task underdeveloped: Much lower F1 scores than intent detection (Table 3), many categories with zero/near-zero performance, 8-category taxonomy not justified. Task feels hastily designed and like an afterthought rather than core contribution.

Statistical rigor gaps: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis. Single evaluation run (temperature=0). Fine-tuning experiments on only 2 models. No error analysis by domain/topic. Missing ablations on component importance (desired influence vs. execution plan).

Incomplete analysis of failures: Limited investigation of why smaller models hallucinate, which manipulations are most deceptive, or why desire inference fails. No breakdown of performance across the 8 influence categories or by topic domain.

strengths: Novel problem framing emphasizing creator intent over surface-level cross-modal misalignment, grounded in communication strategy theory
Large-scale benchmark (12,000 instances) with thorough human evaluation (99.2% text accuracy, high inter-annotator agreement) and validation of realism and intent alignment
Comprehensive VLM analysis revealing concrete weaknesses: over-reliance on image-text consistency, susceptibility to stylistic cues, and vulnerability to spurious authenticity hints
Well-documented methodology with detailed experimental setup, multiple reasoning paradigms (implication vs. consistency-oriented), and analysis across diverse models
Transfer learning experiments demonstrating broader utility for general multimodal misinformation detection
weaknesses: Entire benchmark is synthetically generated (GPT-4o + FLUX.1) with no validation against real-world misinformation; unclear whether synthetic patterns capture authentic deception strategies or represent meaningful phenomena
Evaluation circularity: GPT-4o both generates ground-truth creator intents and is evaluated as one of 14 VLMs, potentially conflating benchmark artifacts with fundamental model limitations
Creator desire inference task has near-zero F1 performance (0-2%) for many models, raising unaddressed questions about ground truth label validity and task meaningfulness
Scope limited to subtle reframing of trustworthy news contexts; does not address broader misinformation phenomena like out-of-context pairings that constitute much real-world deception
Core findings (VLMs rely on stylistic cues and surface-level consistency) align with existing literature; limited conceptual novelty beyond the benchmark resource itself
Modest transfer learning improvements (7.96-30.70pp on MMFakeBench) with final accuracy only 67.24%; lacks ablations comparing intent-focused training to alternative data approaches
Generation prompts withheld 'for safety' significantly harms reproducibility; no sensitivity analysis on filtering criteria or intent taxonomy design
Paper acknowledges bypassing safety guardrails to generate realistic misinformation at scale; ethical concerns inadequately addressed beyond access restrictions

Weak experimental validation: only 2% of data human-evaluated, no statistical significance testing, no error analysis by intent type, limited sample sizes for some studies (e.g., n=200 for image generation comparison)

No comparison to real-world misinformation campaigns to establish whether poor VLM performance reflects actual limitations or benchmark artifacts; restricted to synthetic creator intents rather than authentic campaigns
